title: Device reset & KV-race analysis - StrataScale deep dive

device reset causes (driver mismatch, kernel panics)
KV cache race and prefetch warmup behavior
on-prem/VPC host config and NIC/PCIe resets

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-03
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marco Alvarez (Redwood), Oliver Grant (StrataScale CTO), Lena Vo (ML Eng), Carlos Mendez (Infra), Nadia Karim (Security)

[00:00:10] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll focus on the device resets and repeated soft oom patterns you've been seeing. Priya and Marco from the eng team are here to help debug.
[00:00:22] Oliver: thanks, yeah we've had production hits three times in the last two weeks, usually under steady concurrent requests, not spikey -- like 120 concurrent streams to the model pool.
[00:00:31] Lena: to add, it's mostly our chat completions workload with prompt histories, so KV cache is hot, and we run a quantized 4-bit variant for cost reasons.
[00:00:40] Priya: ok, great context. quick Q: when device reset happens, do you see the CUDA OOM in the model logs first, or a kernel-level device-reset?
[00:00:49] Carlos: logs are a little messy, but usually we see a GPU OOM inside the runtime, then about 10-20s later the node reports a device reset, and our infra restarts the inference container. sometimes dmesg shows a pcie link retrain or 'NVRM: Xid' messages.
[00:01:05] Marco: Xid codes are helpful; can you paste one?
[00:01:10] Carlos: yes here - 'NVRM: Xid 79' (I think).
[00:01:15] Priya: ok Xid 79 is often memory access on kernel or bad page, but we'd need the driver and CUDA versions. Also important: are you using persistent worker processes with warm KV cache or short-lived pods?
[00:01:27] Lena: persistent workers, yes — we keep processes warm and rely on KV cache to avoid re-encoding prefixes.
[00:01:33] Jordan: that's likely why you see soft OOMs — when memory climbs due to KV growth across many sessions and batching spikes it can cross a threshold. The device reset suggests the GPU driver hit something it couldn't recover from.
[00:01:44] Oliver: our guess was a race when the KV cache prefetch runs concurrently with a batch allocation; maybe when the cache grows it triggers fragmentation. We also noticed some runs where quantized kernels allocate a larger scratch buffer.
[00:01:57] Priya: yes, quantization can change workspace requirements. In some kernels 4-bit packing introduces a transposed workspace to run faster, which increases peak ephemeral memory. If that combines with a KV prefetch that tries to pin a large chunk, you can see transient oversubscription — soft OOM followed by driver reset.
[00:02:11] [00:02:30] Jordan: quick note — transcripts sometimes show K V 'cash' in our logs; I'll read it as KV cache.
[00:02:37] Carlos: haha, yes we've seen 'K V cash' in the auto transcripts too.
[00:02:45] Priya: concrete steps to triage: we want the exact Xid, driver version (nvidia-smi -a), CUDA toolkit, and kernel logs. Also, please capture the runtime memory timeline from our /metrics endpoint — that helps correlate allocations with time.
[00:03:00] Lena: we can get that. also curious about retry semantics — right now we do immediate retry twice with no backoff, which probably worsens the wave.
[00:03:09] Marco: yes, immediate retries amplify pressure. For production we recommend a jittered exponential backoff with circuit-breaker: e.g., start at 250ms, x2 up to 4s, and trip the circuit after 3 consecutive device resets to avoid flapping.
[00:03:22] [00:03:45] Oliver: what about KV eviction policies — we currently keep prefetched prefixes for 48 hours. Is there a setting to proactively evict long-tail sessions?
[00:03:55] Priya: yes we have eviction TTL and an LRU cap per-device. For high-concurrency workloads we recommend lowering TTL to 15-30 minutes and setting a soft cap on total KV bytes per model instance; also enable prefix-sharing for identical user contexts if you can canonicalize keys.
[00:04:09] Carlos: is there a runtime flag to disable prefetch during heavy batching windows? we tried a manual throttle but it's crude.
[00:04:17] Priya: not a single switch, but our latest runtime exposes prefetch_rate_limit and prefetch_window_size. Set prefetch_rate_limit to something like 50MB/s and window_size to 64 tokens to smooth memory growth. We'll share the runbook with exact flags.
[00:04:31] Jordan: also worth noting PCIe resets in dmesg sometimes come from NIC interrupts — how is your network topology for private deployment?
[00:04:40] Carlos: it's a VPC with 100Gb RDMA NICs to an on-prem-ish host. We did see a firmware update last month but didn't think it was related.
[00:04:48] Marco: firmware/drivers matter. Mismatched CUDA/driver builds or older NV driver with newer kernels can surface as Xid 79 or 31. We'll provide a matrix of validated driver/CUDA/OS combos.
[00:04:59] [00:05:20] Lena: regarding quantization — could we try the 8-bit fallback for a sample bucket to see if the OOM disappears? We could A/B both quant levels.
[00:05:28] Priya: absolutely. Quantization sometimes trades compute for memory; 8-bit may have larger model params but smaller scratch in certain kernels — odd but true. We'll help set up throughput comparison and a perf/regression test.
[00:05:40] Oliver: what about retry semantics inside Redwood runtime — if a request errors mid-token do you return partial and bubble up?
[00:05:49] Marco: current behavior is to propagate an error and optionally stream what was generated up until the failure; for customer-facing stability we recommend idempotent request patterns and resumable cursors. Also backoff before resubmitting to avoid thrash.
[00:06:03] [00:06:30] Carlos: ok let's talk instrumentation — what traces/logs are most useful?
[00:06:36] Priya: we need 1) runtime allocation timeline (per-process GPU memory metrics at 1s resolution), 2) kvcache perf metrics (entries, bytes, hits/misses), 3) kernel crash Xid with full dmesg around the timestamp, 4) container logs + core dumps if allowed, 5) nvidia-smi -q at the moment. Prefer all zipped.
[00:06:53] Jordan: also include request ids to correlate spikes to customer sessions. If you can run a stress harness with synthetic requests that mirror production concurrency that helps repro.
[00:07:05] Lena: we can script that. question on node sizing — is there guidance on letting one model span multiple GPUs vs pinning per-GPU?
[00:07:14] Marco: for low-latency chat we recommend single-GPU shards with KV cache per process; multi-GPU sharding increases cross-GPU comms and can worsen pcie pressure unless you're using an NCCL-optimized kernels and NVLink. For your 100Gb RDMA setup, single-GPU workers with pooling is a safer default.
[00:07:31] [00:07:55] Oliver: any quick wins we can apply before the repro window?
[00:07:58] Priya: yes — 1) lower KV TTL to 30m, 2) add jittered exponential backoff on client retries, 3) temporarily switch a percent of traffic to 8-bit quantized model, 4) limit concurrent batches per worker (throttle to 80 concurrent). These reduce pressure while we debug root cause.
[00:08:20] Carlos: we'll apply those this week and report.
[00:08:25] [00:30:00] (longer troubleshooting segment with live logs)
[00:30:05] Carlos: uploading sample dmesg: 'NVRM: Xid (79) 13' and 'GPU at 0000:65:00.0: driver error'. Also saw 'GPU page fault' in one trace.
[00:30:18] Priya: thanks — page fault plus Xid 79 strongly suggests a kernel/driver boundary issue; still possible it's memory corruption triggered by a user-pace race.
[00:30:28] Jordan: we noticed some customers hit the issue when running prefetch + async-kv writes during batch compaction. There's a small window where a background eviction and a prefetch compete for the same buffer.
[00:30:37] Lena: could that be a bug in the eviction lock? we recently upgraded the runtime and maybe that change exposed a concurrency path.
[00:30:45] Priya: possible. We'll instrument lock ownership and add additional checks. For now, we can gate prefetch with a soft mutex per-shard to prevent concurrent growth. It's a cheap mitigation.
[00:30:59] Marco: if you can reproduce with our repro harness we can run ASAN or UBSAN-like tools in user space to catch UAFs, though in GPU kernels that's harder — but driver logs will show illegal memory access.
[00:31:12] [00:40:00] (discussion of reproducibility and scheduling follow-up)
[00:40:05] Oliver: security question — if we send device logs and core dumps to Redwood, can you confirm data handling and retention?
[00:40:15] Jordan: yes we'll handle them under our data processing agreement; logs will be limited to debug purposes and deleted after the troubleshooting window — we'll follow your security team's checklist. Nadia: any specific requirements?
[00:40:28] Nadia: just ensure PII isn't included and that we get an ETA on deletion. Also need SOC2 artifacts for our compliance team.
[00:40:35] Jordan: we'll attach SOC 2 and the temporary access plan in the follow-up email.
[00:40:44] [00:55:00] (wrap up and recap)
[00:55:01] Jordan: recap — StrataScale will run the stress harness and collect logs (Carlos). Redwood will share the KV prefetch flags, driver/CUDA matrix, and the repro script (Priya, Marco). We'll meet live during repro week to watch logs. We also recommended immediate mitigations (lower KV TTL, backoff, 8-bit sample).
[00:55:20] Oliver: that sounds good. thanks for the level of detail.
[00:55:26] Priya: we'll attach example config patches and the runbook to the follow-up. Expect links to Gists.
[00:55:34] Jordan: I'll send the calendar invite for the follow-up and include the action items.
[00:55:40] Carlos: thanks all, we'll start collecting and share before Friday.
[00:55:45] Jordan: great, talk soon.

Action items (verbally recapped):
- Run stress harness and collect kernel and runtime logs (Carlos)
- Redwood to share prefetch flags, driver matrix, repro script (Priya/Marco)
- Schedule live troubleshooting session (Jordan)
